## Two kinds of plot

::: {.callout-note title="Exploratory"}
You know what's in it before you look. You make it, take a glance at it, and then move on. You'll make hundreds and discard most.
:::

::: {.callout-caution title="Expository"}
Someone else has to read it, especially someone without your background and without much patience.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
Getting from the first to the second takes real effort. This chapter is the
toolkit.
:::

## Setup

These are the libraries that we are going to use in today's lecture.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(tidyverse)
library(scales)     # label and break helpers
library(ggrepel)    # non-overlapping text labels
library(patchwork)  # combining plots
```
:::



# Labels

## `labs()`


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = class)) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  labs(
    x = "Engine displacement (L)",
    y = "Highway fuel economy (mpg)",
    color = "Car type",
    title = "Fuel efficiency generally decreases with engine size",
    subtitle = "Two seaters are an exception because of their light weight",
    caption = "Data from fueleconomy.gov"
  )
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](DATA100-F26-Lecture-6_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


## What each label is for

| Label | Job |
|---|---|
| `title` | State the **finding**, not the plot's contents |
| `subtitle` | Add detail below the title |
| `caption` | Usually the data source |
| `x`, `y` | Replace variable names with **descriptions** **and units** |
| aesthetic names | Same, for each legend |


## Mathematical labels

Swap the string for `quote()`; see `?plotmath` for the vocabulary.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
df <- tibble(x = 1:10, y = cumsum(x^2))

ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    x = quote(x[i]),
    y = quote(sum(x[i] ^ 2, i == 1, n))
  )
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](DATA100-F26-Lecture-6_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


## Your turn {.smaller}

::: {.callout-note title="The `mpg` variables you'll need"}
| Variable | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `cty` | city fuel economy, in miles per gallon |
| `hwy` | highway fuel economy, in miles per gallon |
| `drv` | drive train: `4` = four-wheel, `f` = front-wheel, `r` = rear-wheel |
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it yourself
Build a scatterplot from `mpg` with `hwy` vs. `cty`, mapping both `color` and `shape` to drive train (`drv`). Add a custom `title`, `subtitle`, `caption`, `x`, and `y` label.
:::


::: {.cell exercise='labels'}

```{.webr .cell-code}
ggplot(mpg, aes(x = cty, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point()
```
:::


# Annotations

## Labelling observations

`geom_text()` is `geom_point()` plus a `label` aesthetic. Build a small data
frame of just the things you want labelled:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
label_info <- mpg |>
  group_by(drv) |>
  arrange(desc(displ)) |>
  slice_head(n = 1) |>
  mutate(
    drive_type = case_when(
      drv == "f" ~ "front-wheel drive",
      drv == "r" ~ "rear-wheel drive",
      drv == "4" ~ "4-wheel drive"
    )
  ) |>
  select(displ, hwy, drv, drive_type)
```
:::


## Labels instead of a legend


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy, color = drv)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  geom_text(
    data = label_info,
    aes(x = displ, y = hwy, label = drive_type),
    fontface = "bold", size = 5, hjust = "right", vjust = "bottom"
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](DATA100-F26-Lecture-6_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::



## `ggrepel` fixes the overlap


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy, color = drv)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  geom_label_repel(
    data = label_info,
    aes(x = displ, y = hwy, label = drive_type),
    fontface = "bold", size = 5, nudge_y = 2
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](DATA100-F26-Lecture-6_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-8-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


## Highlighting specific points



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
potential_outliers <- mpg |> filter(hwy > 40 | (hwy > 20 & displ > 5))

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_text_repel(data = potential_outliers, aes(label = model)) +
  geom_point(data = potential_outliers, color = "red") +
  geom_point(
    data = potential_outliers,
    color = "red", size = 3, shape = "circle open"
  )
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](DATA100-F26-Lecture-6_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-9-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


## Other annotation geoms

::: {.callout-note}
- `geom_hline()` / `geom_vline()` are reference lines. Thick and white (`linewidth = 2, color = "white"`), drawn *under* the data, reads clearly without competing with it
- `geom_rect()` boxes off a region with `xmin`/`xmax`/`ymin`/`ymax`. 
- `geom_segment(arrow = ...)` point at something. `x`/`y` start,
  `xend`/`yend` end
:::


## `annotate()` for one-off text

Geoms highlight *subsets of data*; `annotate()` adds *individual elements*
without needing a data frame.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
trend_text <- "Larger engine sizes tend to have lower fuel economy." |>
  str_wrap(width = 30)

trend_text
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "Larger engine sizes tend to\nhave lower fuel economy."
```


:::
:::


`str_wrap()` inserts line breaks at a chosen width.

## Text plus arrow


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point() +
  annotate(
    geom = "label", x = 3.5, y = 38,
    label = trend_text, hjust = "left", color = "red"
  ) +
  annotate(
    geom = "segment",
    x = 3, y = 35, xend = 5, yend = 25, color = "red",
    arrow = arrow(type = "closed")
  )
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](DATA100-F26-Lecture-6_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-11-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::



## Your turn {.smaller}

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it yourself
1. Use `geom_text()` with infinite positions to place text in all four
   corners.
2. Use `annotate()` to drop a single customized point in the middle of a plot.
:::


::: {.cell exercise='annotations'}

```{.webr .cell-code}
ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_text(x = -Inf, y = Inf, label = "Top left", hjust = 0, vjust = 1) +
  geom_text(x = Inf, y = Inf, label = "Top right", hjust = 1, vjust = 1) +
  geom_text(x = -Inf, y = -Inf, label = "Bottom left", hjust = 0, vjust = 0) +
  geom_text(x = Inf, y = -Inf, label = "Bottom right", hjust = 1, vjust = 0) + 
  annotate(
    geom = "point", x = 4, y = 25,
    color = "red", size = 4, shape = 8
  )
```
:::


## Your turn {.smaller}

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it yourself

Run the following code with `geom_text()` that draws its label data into every matching facet. If your label data frame has a column matching the faceting variable, `ggplot2` only places that label in the facet(s) where the value matches. Try labeling just the cyl = 8 facet, then try giving every facet its own distinct label.

:::


::: {.cell exercise='annotations'}

```{.webr .cell-code}
labels <- tibble(
  cyl = c(4, 5, 6, 8),
  displ = 6, hwy = 40,
  label = c("4 cyl", "5 cyl", "6 cyl", "8 cyl")
)

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_text(data = labels, aes(label = label)) +
  facet_wrap(~cyl)
```
:::


# Scales

## Scales are always there

These two produce identical output:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = class))

ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = class)) +
  scale_x_continuous() +
  scale_y_continuous() +
  scale_color_discrete()
```
:::


Naming scheme: `scale_` + aesthetic + `_` + scale type
(`continuous`, `discrete`, `date`, `datetime`).

## Two reasons to override

1. **Tweak the default**: different breaks, different labels
2. **Replace it entirely**: a transformation or palette that fits your data
   better than a general-purpose default can

## Breaks and labels

Axes and legends are collectively called **guides**. 

- `breaks` sets where the ticks or keys go
- `labels` sets what they say


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy, color = drv)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(15, 40, by = 5))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](DATA100-F26-Lecture-6_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-15-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


## Suppressing and renaming

`labels = NULL` removes the labels entirely


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy, color = drv)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = NULL) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = NULL) +
  scale_color_discrete(labels = c("4" = "4-wheel", "f" = "front", "r" = "rear"))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](DATA100-F26-Lecture-6_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-16-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::



## Formatting with the scales package


::: {.cell layout-ncol="2"}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = price, y = cut)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.05) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_dollar())
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](DATA100-F26-Lecture-6_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-17-1.png){width=432}
:::

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = price, y = cut)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.05) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    labels = label_dollar(scale = 1/1000, suffix = "K"),
    breaks = seq(1000, 19000, by = 6000)
  )
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](DATA100-F26-Lecture-6_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-17-2.png){width=432}
:::
:::


Note `breaks` stays in the original data scale.

## Percentages


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = cut, fill = clarity)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  scale_y_continuous(name = "Percentage", labels = label_percent())
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](DATA100-F26-Lecture-6_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-18-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


## Breaks that mark real events

With few data points, put the ticks where the observations are:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
presidential |>
  mutate(id = 33 + row_number()) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = start, y = id)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = end, yend = id)) +
  scale_x_date(name = NULL, breaks = presidential$start, date_labels = "'%y")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](DATA100-F26-Lecture-6_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-19-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


Dates use `date_labels` (a format string) and `date_breaks` (`"2 days"`,`"1 month"`).

## Legend position

`legend.position` is a **theme** setting:


::: {.cell layout-ncol="2"}

```{.r .cell-code}
base <- ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) + geom_point(aes(color = class))

base + theme(legend.position = "right")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](DATA100-F26-Lecture-6_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-20-1.png){width=432}
:::

```{.r .cell-code}
base + theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  guides(color = guide_legend(nrow = 3))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](DATA100-F26-Lecture-6_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-20-2.png){width=432}
:::
:::


Short and wide → top or bottom. Tall and narrow → left or right.`"none"` removes it.

## Overriding legend aesthetics


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = class)) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  guides(color = guide_legend(nrow = 2, override.aes = list(size = 4)))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](DATA100-F26-Lecture-6_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-21-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


## Transform in the scale, not the mapping


::: {.cell layout-ncol="2"}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = log10(carat), y = log10(price))) +
  geom_bin2d()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](DATA100-F26-Lecture-6_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-22-1.png){width=432}
:::

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = carat, y = price)) +
  geom_bin2d() +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_y_log10()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](DATA100-F26-Lecture-6_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-22-2.png){width=432}
:::
:::


::: {.callout-note}
Visually identical — but the right-hand axes are labelled in the *original*
units. Transforming inside `aes()` leaves the reader staring at log values;
transforming via the scale keeps the plot interpretable.
:::

##ColorBrewer

The default categorical palette spaces hues evenly around the color wheel. ColorBrewer's palettes are hand-tuned so common forms of color blindness can still distinguish them.


::: {.cell layout-ncol="2"}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) + geom_point(aes(color = drv))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](DATA100-F26-Lecture-6_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-23-1.png){width=432}
:::

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = drv)) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](DATA100-F26-Lecture-6_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-23-2.png){width=432}
:::
:::



## Predetermined mapping

Some variables come with expected colors. `scale_color_manual()` pins them down to the specific colour:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
presidential |>
  mutate(id = 33 + row_number()) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = start, y = id, color = party)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = end, yend = id)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(Republican = "#E81B23", Democratic = "#00AEF3"))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](DATA100-F26-Lecture-6_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-24-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::



## Three ways to set limits

1. Filter the data
2. Set `limits` on the scale
3. Set `xlim`/`ylim` in `coord_cartesian()`

::: {.callout-caution}
Options 1 and 2 both throw data away before any stat or smooth is fit 
 - a `geom_smooth()` curve will genuinely change shape. 

Option 3 is a true zoom: the smooth is fit on the full data and only the *view* changes. Pick option 3 unless you actually want to refit on a subset.
:::

## What do i mean by that?


::: {.cell layout-ncol="2"}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = drv)) + geom_smooth() +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(5, 6)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(10, 25))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](DATA100-F26-Lecture-6_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-25-1.png){width=432}
:::

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = drv)) + geom_smooth() +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(5, 6), ylim = c(10, 25))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](DATA100-F26-Lecture-6_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-25-2.png){width=432}
:::
:::


Same window, different smooth curves.

## An even simpler example


::: {.cell exercise='simple zoom'}

```{.webr .cell-code}
set.seed(123)

cluster_a <- tibble(
  x = runif(15, 0, 3),
  y = 10 - 2 * x + rnorm(15, sd = 1)
)
cluster_b <- tibble(
  x = runif(200, 3, 10),
  y = 4 + 1.5 * x + rnorm(200, sd = 3)
)
df <- bind_rows(cluster_a, cluster_b)

# General plot
ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm")

# Filtering/limits: refits on ONLY the points in view
ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 3))

# coord_cartesian: keeps the original full-data line, just crops the view
ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 3))

```
:::



## Expanding limits to share scales {.smaller}

`limits` is genuinely useful in the other direction: making separate plots
comparable.


::: {.cell layout-ncol="2"}

```{.r .cell-code}
suv     <- mpg |> filter(class == "suv")
compact <- mpg |> filter(class == "compact")

x_scale   <- scale_x_continuous(limits = range(mpg$displ))
y_scale   <- scale_y_continuous(limits = range(mpg$hwy))
col_scale <- scale_color_discrete(limits = unique(mpg$drv))

ggplot(suv, aes(displ, hwy, color = drv)) +
  geom_point() + x_scale + y_scale + col_scale
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](DATA100-F26-Lecture-6_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-27-1.png){width=432}
:::

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(compact, aes(displ, hwy, color = drv)) +
  geom_point() + x_scale + y_scale + col_scale
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](DATA100-F26-Lecture-6_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-27-2.png){width=432}
:::
:::



# Themes

## Built-in themes


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = class)) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  theme_bw()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](DATA100-F26-Lecture-6_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-28-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


Eight ship with ggplot2: `theme_gray()` (default), `theme_bw()`, `theme_light()`, `theme_classic()`, `theme_linedraw()`, `theme_dark()`, `theme_minimal()`, `theme_void()`. The package **ggthemes** adds many more.



## Customizing individual components

`theme()` controls everything non-data. `element_*()` functions describe how
each piece looks.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy, color = drv)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Larger engine sizes tend to have lower fuel economy",
    caption = "Source: https://fueleconomy.gov."
  ) +
  theme(
    legend.position = c(0.6, 0.7),
    legend.direction = "horizontal",
    legend.box.background = element_rect(color = "black"),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.title.position = "plot",
    plot.caption.position = "plot",
    plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0)
  )
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](DATA100-F26-Lecture-6_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-29-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


## Try it


::: {.cell exercise='theme'}

```{.webr .cell-code}
ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy, color = drv)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    title = "Larger engine sizes tend to have lower fuel economy",
    caption = "Source: https://fueleconomy.gov."
  ) +
  theme(
    legend.position = c(0.6, 0.7),
    legend.direction = "horizontal",
    legend.box.background = element_rect(color = "black"),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.title.position = "plot",
    plot.caption.position = "plot",
    plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0)
  )

```
:::



## Worth knowing

- `element_text()`: font face, size, color, justification
- `element_rect()`: backgrounds and borders
- `element_line()`: grid lines and axis lines
- `element_blank()`: remove a component entirely

`plot.title.position = "plot"` aligns the title to the whole graphic rather
than the panel, which usually looks better with left-aligned captions.

See `?theme` for the full list.

# Layout

## patchwork

Save plots as objects, then combine with operators:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
p1 <- ggplot(mpg, aes(x = displ, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point() + labs(title = "Plot 1")
p2 <- ggplot(mpg, aes(x = drv, y = hwy)) +
  geom_boxplot() + labs(title = "Plot 2")

p1 + p2
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](DATA100-F26-Lecture-6_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-31-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


patchwork doesn't add a new function here!

## Composing layouts

`|` places side by side, `/` starts a new row.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
p3 <- ggplot(mpg, aes(x = cty, y = hwy)) +
  geom_point() + labs(title = "Plot 3")

(p1 | p3) / p2
```

## Collecting legends


::: {.cell exercise='layouts'}

```{.webr .cell-code}
p1 <- ggplot(mpg, aes(drv, cty, color = drv)) +
  geom_boxplot(show.legend = FALSE) + labs(title = "Plot 1")
p2 <- ggplot(mpg, aes(drv, hwy, color = drv)) +
  geom_boxplot(show.legend = FALSE) + labs(title = "Plot 2")
p3 <- ggplot(mpg, aes(cty, color = drv, fill = drv)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.5) + labs(title = "Plot 3")
p4 <- ggplot(mpg, aes(hwy, color = drv, fill = drv)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.5) + labs(title = "Plot 4")
p5 <- ggplot(mpg, aes(cty, hwy, color = drv)) +
  geom_point(show.legend = FALSE) + facet_wrap(~drv) + labs(title = "Plot 5")

(guide_area() / (p1 + p2) / (p3 + p4) / p5) +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "City and highway mileage for cars with different drive trains",
    caption = "Source: https://fueleconomy.gov."
  ) +
  plot_layout(guides = "collect", heights = c(1, 3, 2, 4)) &
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```
:::


## What just happened

- `guide_area()` reserves a slot for the shared legend
- `plot_layout(guides = "collect")` gathers legends from every panel into it
- `heights = c(1, 3, 2, 4)` divides the vertical space proportionally

::: {.callout-note}
`&` applies a theme setting to **every** plot in the patchwork; a plain `+` would only affect the last one added. This is the one place in ggplot2 code where `&` and `+` are not interchangeable.
:::

## Summary

- **Labels**: the title states the finding; axes carry units
- **Annotations**: `geom_text()` for data, `annotate()` for one-offs; reference lines, rectangles, and arrows
- **Scales**: `breaks` and `labels` to tweak, whole scales to replace;
  transform in the scale so axes stay readable
- **Color**: ColorBrewer and viridis for accessibility; redundant shape
  encoding is free insurance
- **Zooming**: `coord_cartesian()` zooms, `limits` subsets
- **Themes**: everything that isn't data
- **Layout**: patchwork for multi-panel figures

  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
